SOURCE: Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL). Adam Zweiger, Jyothish Pari, Han Guo, Ekin Akyürek, Yoon Kim, Pulkit Agrawal (MIT). 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025), arXiv:2506.10943v2 [cs.LG], 18 Sep 2025. The PDF text confirms the venue.

COVERAGE: 84158 of 84158 chars (25 pages: main text, limitations, references skimmed, appendices A and B in full). Extracted text saved at /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/seal/seal_text.txt. Figures 4 and 6 are plots and I did not look at the images. Their numbers come from text and tables only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- SEAL trains a model to write its own finetuning data ("self-edits"). An outer RL loop rewards self-edits by the post-SFT accuracy of the updated model, and an inner loop applies the SFT update.
  number: none
  setup: a framework paper with two instantiations, knowledge incorporation (Qwen2.5-7B) and ARC few-shot (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct).
  quote: "SEAL can therefore be interpreted as an algorithm with two nested loops: an outer RL loop, which optimizes the self-edit generation, and an inner update loop, which uses the generated self-edit to update the model via gradient descent."
  where: p.3, §3

- Single-passage knowledge incorporation rises from 33.5% (passage only) to 47.0% after RL, above GPT-4.1 synthetic data at 46.3%.
  number: 33.5% -> 47.0%; GPT-4.1 46.3%
  setup: Qwen2.5-7B, no-passage SQuAD v1.1, one passage per LoRA update, 2 rounds of ReST-EM. Each round uses 50 contexts with 5 self-edits each. Grader is GPT-4.1 on a 200-passage eval subset (974 questions).
  quote: "finetuning on self-generated synthetic data improves question-answering performance on the no-passage-in-context variant of SQuAD [13] from 33.5% to 47.0%. Notably, self-generated data from SEAL outperforms synthetic data generated by GPT-4.1."
  where: p.2, §1. Table 2 on p.8 gives the base model 32.7, passage only 33.5, passage plus base-model synthetic 39.7, GPT-4.1 46.3, SEAL 47.0.

- Continued pretraining (many passages, full finetuning) does not beat GPT-4.1 data and is below it at n=2067. SEAL beats the base-model-synthetic baseline at both sizes.
  number: n=200: SEAL 58.2 vs GPT-4.1 59.4. n=2067: SEAL 46.4 vs GPT-4.1 49.2.
  setup: Qwen2.5-7B, full finetuning, 5 self-edits per passage aggregated. Same SQuAD no-context eval. Table 2 gives passage plus synthetic (base model, no RL) as 50.6 at n=200 and 43.4 at n=2067.
  quote: "we observe a similar ranking of methods as in the single-passage case, but with synthetic data from GPT-4.1 slightly outperforming SEAL."
  where: p.7-8, Table 2

- ARC few-shot success rate is 72.5% with SEAL, against 20% for self-edits without RL and 0% for ICL. It stays below the oracle TTT configuration at 100%.
  number: 72.5 / 20 / 0 / 100
  setup: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Tiny curated set: 11 ARC training tasks for RL and 8 evaluation tasks, filtered to be solvable with optimal TTT. 15 self-edits per training task. At evaluation, 5 self-edits per task, 40 configurations in total, and success is the percentage of configurations that are correct. ReST-EM ran a single outer loop, about 2-3 h on one A100/H100/H200.
  quote: "SEAL substantially improves adaptation success rate compared to baselines: 72.5% vs. 20% (with self-edits from the base model without RL training) and 0% (no adaptation), though performance remains below Oracle TTT"
  where: p.6-7, Table 1; setup in App. A.1-A.4

- The RL loop saturates fast. Two ReST-EM iterations suffice to pass GPT-4.1 data, and later iterations give diminishing returns.
  number: 2 iterations
  setup: knowledge incorporation, Qwen2.5-7B (Fig. 4)
  quote: "Two iterations suffice for SEAL to overtake GPT-4.1 data; subsequent iterations yield diminishing returns"
  where: p.7

- Algorithm choice: GRPO and PPO were unstable, so the authors use ReST-EM (rejection sampling plus SFT). The reward is binary, and training must be on-policy because the reward depends on the current weights.
  number: none
  quote: "We experimented with various on-policy methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [66] and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [67], but found the training to be unstable."
  where: p.4. Also "we adopt an on-policy approach, in which self-edits are sampled from—and, crucially, rewards are computed using—the current model."
  Reward (eq. 2): 1 if adaptation using SE improves performance on τ, else 0. For knowledge incorporation, only the single best of the sampled self-edits is rewarded (footnote 2).

- Cost per outer-loop iteration is high. One self-edit evaluation takes about 30-45 s. One ReST-EM round is 750 inner-loop iterations (50 passages x 5 completions x 3 seeds), taking about 6 h on 2xH100.
  number: 30-45 s per self-edit; 750 inner iterations; about 6 hr
  quote: "each self-edit evaluation takes approximately 30–45 seconds, introducing substantial overhead (see §B.5)." And: "Doing a single round requires a batch of 50 passages over 5 completions and 3 runs per completion, meaning 750 inner loop iterations. This takes about 6 hours on 2×H100s."
  where: p.9 (§5); App. B.5, p.21

- A cheap proxy reward cuts RL training time sharply and loses little accuracy.
  number: 47.0 (about 6 hr) vs 45.6 (about 5 min)
  setup: knowledge incorporation. Proxy is a GPT-4.1 rubric on length, diversity, quality and correctness, each scored 1-5 and summed. The base is 32.0 in this table.
  quote: "SEAL 32.0 47.0 ≈6 hr / SEAL w/ Proxy-Reward 32.0 45.6 ≈5 min"
  where: App. B.10, Table 9, p.23

- RL gives roughly the same absolute gain across several self-edit prompts, and the paper warns that outcomes are prompt-sensitive.
  number: "roughly 6 to 11 percentage points"
  setup: single-document knowledge incorporation, 2 rounds, 7 prompt formats (Table 10, p.24). Examples: implications 39.7 -> 47.0; rewrite 49.4 -> 55.6; self-qa 37.3 -> 48.7; no-prompt 13.8 -> 18.9, which is below GPT-4.1's 28.6.
  quote: "In all cases, ReSTEM enhanced performance by roughly 6 to 11 percentage points."
  where: App. B.11, p.23

- The RL gain is larger at 7B than at 3B, but the authors say this is weak evidence.
  number: 1.75x (3B) vs 2.04x (7B)
  setup: single-passage, Qwen2.5-3B: base 25.1, base-model self-edit 31.9, SEAL 37.0. Qwen2.5-7B: 32.7, 39.7, 47.0.
  quote: "This ratio is 1.75× for the 3B model and 2.04× for the 7B model."
  where: App. B.7, p.21-22. "We acknowledge that it is hard to draw conclusions though without actually scaling up further."

- Against Generative Adapter (a hypernetwork), SEAL loses single-passage but wins at CPT.
  number: single-passage 47.0 vs 66.8; CPT n=200 58.2 vs 28.0
  setup: Generative Adapter uses a Mistral-7B model, SEAL uses Qwen2.5-7B. The "Base" column is 32.0 for SEAL and 24.4 for Generative Adapter.
  where: Table 7, App. B.8, p.22.
  Quote check: the extraction merges the columns ("Generative Adapter 24.466.828.0"), so the 66.8 reading is inferred from the column layout. No clean quote.

- Entigraph (pairs plus triples, 10 generations) is competitive with SEAL, which used 5 generations.
  number: n=200: SEAL 58.2 vs 56.0; n=2067: SEAL 46.4 vs 48.6
  quote: "Entigraph with all 10 synthetic data generations sampling is competitive with SEAL, especially at the larger scale."
  where: App. B.9, Table 8, p.22-23

LIMITS
- Catastrophic forgetting is not addressed. The authors did not optimise for retention. In the continual setting, performance on earlier passages declines as more self-edits are applied. There is no numeric value in the text, only Fig. 6 and the SEM table.
  quote: "performance on earlier tasks gradually declines as the number of edits increases, suggesting that SEAL is still susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. Still, it can perform multiple updates without complete collapse"
  where: p.9
  Setup: knowledge-incorporation stream of passages (the table in App. B.6 suggests 8 passages and 8 edits). Proposed fixes are untested: reward shaping against regressions, null-space constrained edits, representational superposition, or RL instead of SFT in the inner loop.
- Compute: each reward needs a finetune plus evaluation of the whole model (see the cost claim above). The authors contrast this with single-forward-pass or regex rewards.
- Context-dependent evaluation: every context needs a paired downstream task (reference QA, or a held-out ARC query). That blocks scaling to unlabeled corpora. The suggested remedy is to have the model write its own evaluation questions, which is not tried.
- The ARC set is tiny (11 training and 8 evaluation tasks, filtered to be solvable), on a 1B model. The paper itself says "While this is a small number of examples".
- Knowledge-incorporation results come from one model family (Qwen2.5 3B/7B) on SQuAD, with a GPT-4.1 grader. Passages are ones the base model can understand in context.
- Teacher-student decoupling is only described, not run.
- The "no-prompt" free-form self-edit format fails: 18.9% after 2 rounds.
- No statistical significance is reported for the headline numbers. SEMs appear only for the forgetting experiment.
- Several of the paper's claims are speculative: the "data wall" argument (Villalobos et al., frontier models trained on all public human text by 2028), agentic self-modification, and pretraining.

BUILDS ON (author, year as printed)
- ReST-EM: Singh et al. [40]. The reference is cited as [40] and I did not read the author name in the text I extracted.
- Test-time training protocol and ARC tools: Akyürek et al. [36].
- Implications-based knowledge injection: Akyürek et al. [30] (deductive closure training); Lampinen et al. [31]; Park et al. [32] (QA prompting); Yang et al. [25] (Entigraph).
- LoRA [72]. GRPO [66] and PPO [67] were tried and abandoned.
- Generative Adapter [54] (Chen et al.); Hu et al. [53].
- Catastrophic forgetting [73, 74]. RL forgets less than SFT [80].
- Self-improvement context: RLAIF [56, 57], self-rewarding LMs [58, 59].
- The reference list was only skimmed. Only the numbered citations appear in the main text, and I did not match all names to numbers.

CODE
- Algorithm 1 (p.4), paraphrased as pseudocode in the source, not copied verbatim:
  - for outer iteration t: sample (C, τ) from D
  - generate SE ~ LM_θ(·|C)
  - inner loop: θ'_t <- SFT(θ_t, SE)
  - evaluate Ans ~ LM_θ'_t(·|τ)
  - compute r <- r(Ans, τ)
  - update: θ_{t+1} <- RL_Update(θ_t, r, SE)
- Reward (eq. 2): r = 1 if adaptation using SE improves LM_θt's performance on τ, else 0.
- Self-edit prompt for knowledge incorporation (App. B.3): "Let's read the following passage and produce a list of implications derived directly or indirectly from the content. Passage: {passage} Implications:"
- ARC self-edit JSON schema (App. A.2, p.19): {"data_generation": {"use_basic_augmentations": ..., "use_size_augmentations": ..., "use_chain_augmentations": ..., "use_repeat_augmentations": ...}, "training": {"strategy": ..., "learning_rate": ..., "num_train_epochs": ...}}
- Hyperparameters for the RL SFT step in knowledge incorporation (B.2): batch size 10, 2 epochs, lr 3e-4, LoRA rank 64, alpha 128.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.2): SEAL overview. Each RL outer-loop iteration generates candidate self-edits, applies them, evaluates on the downstream task and reinforces. Shows the nested-loop structure at a glance.
- Fig. 4 (p.7): accuracy over RL iterations against the baselines (raw passage, Qwen-base synthetic, GPT-4.1 synthetic). Shows SEAL crossing GPT-4.1 by iteration 2.
- Fig. 5 (p.8): example self-edits across RL iterations. RL leads to longer and more detailed self-edits, and the authors say the differences are sometimes subtler.
- Fig. 6 (p.8): catastrophic forgetting from continual self-edits, a heatmap of earlier-task accuracy over edits.

PROBLEMS
- The scratch file name t.txt collided. Another session writing to /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/t.txt overwrote my extraction with an unrelated AlphaEvolve paper (Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner). I discarded that text and re-extracted the SEAL PDF into /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/seal/seal_text.txt. The PDF metadata and the full extraction there are SEAL. All claims above come from that clean extraction.
- Table columns in the extraction are merged for some bolded cells (Tables 2, 6, 7, 8), for example "46.359.4 49.2". I split them using the column layout. The Generative Adapter 66.8 and SEAL 47.0/58.2 values are inferred from that layout.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- Not in the paper: the number of self-edits per outer iteration beyond the stated 50x5x3 seeds for knowledge incorporation, and any per-iteration dollar cost. Cost is only given as GPU time.
